candidates.attacker_control: Any value the calling application feeds into Commandline.createArg()/createArgument()/addArguments(String[]) (e.g. file names, URLs, paths, user-supplied tool options), into Commandline.setExecutable(String) (tool paths resolved from configuration/user input), or into Commandline.setWorkingDirectory(String) (e.g. a configured build directory), for any consumer that uses BourneShell/Commandline/CommandLineUtils.executeCommandLine.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: BourneShell does apply real quoting/escaping for the common cases: arguments containing space, $, ;, &, |, <, >, *, ?, (), [], {} or backtick are wrapped in single quotes and embedded single quotes are escaped as '\'' (escape pattern `'\%s'`, BourneShell.java:58-63), so simple payloads such as `x; id` or `$(id)` are neutralized; the default Shell/CmdShell likewise adds double quotes for arguments containing spaces. The bypasses are limited to (a) arguments that start and end with the quote character (early return in quoteAndEscape), (b) characters absent from both the trigger and escape sets (notably newline; also $/backtick/quote when used inside the executable or preamble where escaping is disabled), and (c) callers explicitly disabling quoting. I verified that MXParser does not process DOCTYPE/external entities (FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL is unsupported and parseDocdecl only scans to '>'), that FileUtils.resolveFile canonicalizes but does not enforce containment, and that no in-repo caller wires these APIs to an untrusted source (no test tree present).
candidates.impact: Arbitrary OS command execution with the privileges of the process using the library (build tool/CI/agent). Depending on those privileges this enables reading or overwriting arbitrary files, exfiltrating credentials, or executing further binaries; in build/CI contexts this typically means full compromise of the build environment.
candidates.prerequisites: The application uses Commandline (default or explicitly BourneShell) or CommandLineUtils.executeCommandLine and passes attacker-influenced text into one of the argument/executable/working-directory APIs. For the cleanest argument vector, an argument whose first and last characters are `'` (e.g. `''; <command>; ''`) is enough; alternatively an argument containing a newline but no other metacharacter (e.g. `name\nid`) is neither escaped nor quoted. Configurations with quotedArgumentsEnabled/quotedExecutableEnabled disabled are directly injectable as well.
candidates.root_cause: Shell.getRawCommandLine (Shell.java:132-178) concatenates shell command, executable, working-directory preamble and arguments into one string that is executed as `/bin/sh -c <string>`. Arguments are passed through StringUtils.quoteAndEscape with only the single-quote character as an escape set and with a quoting-trigger list that omits newline; moreover quoteAndEscape short-circuits and returns the input unchanged when it merely starts and ends with the quote character (StringUtils.java:2314-2318), so an argument such as `''; <command>; ''` is emitted verbatim into the sh -c string. BourneShell (BourneShell.java:32-48, 55-69) also wraps the executable in double quotes while disabling both single- and double-quoted executable escaping (getEscapeChars returns an empty set, Shell.java:190-207), so `$`, backtick and `"` inside the executable remain active, and getExecutionPreamble/unifyQuotes (BourneShell.java:118-133, 157-170) interpolates the working directory with a fallback (StringUtils.escape) that leaves `$`, `;`, `&`, `|`, backtick and parentheses unescaped. Any shell command character that is neither in the trigger list nor in the escape set can therefore terminate/alter the intended command.
candidates.title: OS command injection through incomplete shell escaping of Commandline arguments/executable/working directory (BourneShell + Shell + StringUtils.quoteAndEscape)
candidates.trace: 1) Commandline.execute() (Commandline.java:618-660) builds the environment and calls Runtime.getRuntime().exec(getShellCommandline(), ...) (Commandline.java:636 or 651). 2) getShellCommandline() (Commandline.java:501-507) delegates to Shell.getShellCommandLine() (Shell.java:266-285), which prepends the shell command and its args (`/bin/sh`, `-c` via BourneShell.getShellArgsList/getShellArgs, BourneShell.java:82-116). 3) getRawCommandLine() (Shell.java:132-178) appends the execution preamble (`cd <workingDir> && ` from BourneShell.getExecutionPreamble/unifyQuotes, BourneShell.java:118-170), then the executable and each argument using StringUtils.quoteAndEscape. 4) For arguments (Shell.java:165-167) the escape set is only {'\''} and the trigger list is BASH_QUOTING_TRIGGER_CHARS (BourneShell.java:32-48) which does not contain '\n'; in StringUtils.quoteAndEscape (StringUtils.java:2303-2349) an argument beginning and ending with `'` is returned unchanged at lines 2314-2318, and an argument with no `'` and no trigger character is returned unquoted at lines 2320-2348. 5) The resulting single string is handed to `/bin/sh -c`, so the embedded `;`/newline (or `$`/backtick left active inside the double-quoted executable/preamble) is interpreted by the shell and the injected command runs with the caller's privileges.
candidates.unverified: No runtime reproduction or dynamic confirmation was performed and no code was executed. The exact consumer that passes attacker-controlled text into Commandline is outside this snapshot (library-only view), so the practical attack surface depends on downstream callers and on JVM/shell behavior; the practical payload space for the argument vector is also constrained by the caller's own validation. Additionally, because the snapshot has no tests, I could not compare against upstream regression tests.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-78 OS Command Injection (improper neutralization of shell metacharacters)

coverage_summary: Scope per get_source_scope: 100 model-visible files, 100 source files, no binary/symlink exclusions, same filters for B0/P1. Per get_relation_scope: the index covers all 100 files (index_status complete, 0 missing, 0 hash mismatches) but is syntactic navigation only (no control/data-flow, runtime reachability, or exploitability proof). Files reviewed in depth: cli package (Shell, BourneShell, CmdShell, CommandShell, Commandline, CommandLineUtils, StreamPumper/Feeder), StringUtils.quoteAndEscape/escape, Expand, FileUtils.resolveFile/createTempFile/copy, DirectoryScanner symlink logic, MXParser docdecl/entity handling, Xpp3DomBuilder, XmlReader/XmlStreamReader, XmlWriterUtil/PrettyPrintXMLWriter, ReflectionValueExtractor, FastMap serialization. The rest of the tree (Base64, TypeFormat, IOUtil, PathTool, SelectorUtils, DAG, SweeperPool, CachedMap, Reader/WriterFactory, introspection/reflection classes, MXSerializer/XmlSerializer, XmlUtil, Xpp3Dom*) was searched with targeted greps for execution/file/URL/deserialization/reflection sinks but not read line-by-line.
limitations: Snapshot contains only main sources (no src/test), so regression tests and upstream patch context could not be inspected.
No build, test, scanner, or exploit execution was performed; the candidate is a source-evidence lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
Downstream consumers of plexus-utils (which determine whether attacker-controlled text actually reaches Commandline/Expand) are outside this snapshot.
The P1 relation index is syntactic only and does not prove reachability, complete data flow, or exploitability; index 'security_call' facts were treated as navigation hints only.
Shell-parsing conclusions are based on reading POSIX /bin/sh semantics; no shell was executed to validate payload behavior.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip Slip / arbitrary file write in Expand.extractFile via FileUtils.resolveFile (Expand.java:112-119 and 145-211; FileUtils.java:1308-1377)
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker-controlled zip entry names are written with new FileOutputStream after FileUtils.resolveFile, and resolveFile canonicalizes but never verifies the result stays under the destination directory (absolute names are returned as-is; ../ escapes). This is a genuine weakness, but it depends on an external caller extracting untrusted archives, no in-repo caller exists, and the snapshot version (3.0.16-SNAPSHOT) and escaping-focused CLI root cause make this the weaker lead; kept as an unconfirmed alternative rather than a second candidate.

MXParser refuses FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL (setFeature throws; getFeature returns false) and parseDocdecl only scans to the matching '>' without resolving external/internal entity declarations; no external-entity resolution path is present, so no source-level XXE evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: XML markup injection via XmlWriterUtil.writeComment / PrettyPrintXMLWriter element names and attributes
rejected_leads.reason: writeComment passes caller text to writeMarkup without filtering '--' and startElement/addAttribute do not validate names, so break-out is possible, but the impact is limited to malformed output and requires the caller to place attacker text in comments/names; no strong evidence of a security boundary being crossed.

rejected_leads.lead: Predictable temporary file names in FileUtils.createTempFile (FileUtils.java:2216-2238)
rejected_leads.reason: Uses a 5-digit java.util.Random-derived suffix and only an exists() check before returning (no file creation), which is a local race/TOCTOU hardening issue; the API documents that it does not create the file and no direct attacker-controlled path/privilege boundary is demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Invocation of getters via ReflectionValueExtractor.evaluate on attacker-controlled expressions
rejected_leads.reason: Expression tokens are restricted to name[digits]/name(key)/get*/is* lookups on the supplied root object; there is no method-name or class-loading sink evident in this snapshot, so no concrete exploit path was established.

summary: Snapshot: plexus-utils 3.0.16-SNAPSHOT main sources (100 files, no tests). After tracing the CLI layer, the strongest evidence-supported issue is a shell command-injection root cause in the command-line construction used by Commandline/BourneShell: attacker-influenced arguments (and, secondarily, executable/working-directory strings) are interpolated into a single `/bin/sh -c` string with incomplete escaping. I also examined the archive-extraction (Expand/FileUtils.resolveFile), XML (MXParser/Xpp3DomBuilder/XmlWriterUtil), FileUtils, DirectoryScanner, StringUtils and introspection areas; the zip-slip and XXE leads are noted as rejected/unconfirmed leads rather than additional candidates. No runtime verification was performed.
